# Exchange across the Americas: sources and route notes

Research checked September 21, 2026. Story copy is in `history/<period>.md`; the geographic route data is in `tour-americas.mjs`.

## Reading the map

Four periods show selected exchanges around 1000 BCE, 400 CE, 1000 CE and 1450 CE. They are not a complete inventory of trade, not political borders, and not a single continuous network. Routes join known sources, workshops or find-sites with schematic corridors along coasts, rivers and highland roads. Where the source of a material is established by geochemistry, archaeology or genetics, the line is drawn at full strength. Where a connection is inferred from imagery, plants, technology or a single find, it is marked uncertain and drawn fainter. Dot frequency is visual timing, not volume.

## Mesoamerica

- [UNESCO: Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/414/) and [UNESCO: Tikal National Park](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/64/). Context for Teotihuacan’s reach into the Maya world around 400 CE. Pachuca green obsidian and Motagua jade are widely sourced materials; their corridors here are schematic.
- Olmec obsidian and jade: highland Guatemalan (El Chayal) and central Mexican obsidian and Motagua-valley jade at Gulf-coast centres such as San Lorenzo and La Venta are established by sourcing studies summarized in general archaeological literature. The exact paths across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec are not known.
- Maize and cacao: [Kistler et al., Science (2018): Multiproxy evidence highlights a complex evolutionary legacy of maize in South America](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aav0207) supports maize reaching South America in partially domesticated form thousands of years before 1000 BCE; the southward crop line therefore spans millennia and is drawn fainter. [Zarrillo et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018): The use and domestication of Theobroma cacao during the mid-Holocene in the upper Amazon](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-018-0697-x) places early cacao use in the Ecuadorian Amazon about 5,300 years ago; the northward cacao line is a hypothesis about how the plant later reached Mesoamerica.
- Aztec and Maya trade: pochteca merchants, Soconusco cacao tribute and Maya coastal canoe trade (including the large trading canoe met by Columbus’s fourth voyage in 1502 off Honduras) are described in standard histories; the drawn merchant routes are representative.

## North America

- [UNESCO: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1689/). Hopewell sites hold obsidian from the Yellowstone region, copper from Lake Superior and marine shell from the Gulf; the corridors are schematic.
- [UNESCO: Cahokia Mounds](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/198/). Cahokia, around 1050–1350 CE, received Gulf shell and northern copper. Later Mississippian towns (Moundville, Spiro, Etowah) continued these exchanges.
- [Crown & Hurst, PNAS (2009): Evidence of cacao use in the Prehispanic American Southwest](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0812817106) and [Watson et al., PNAS (2015): Early procurement of scarlet macaws and the emergence of social complexity in Chaco Canyon](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1509825112). Cacao residues and macaw remains at [Chaco Canyon](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/353/) show Mesoamerican goods reaching the Southwest by about 1000 CE. The corridor between them is unknown and is drawn fainter.
- [UNESCO: Archaeological Zone of Paquimé, Casas Grandes](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/560/). Paquimé bred scarlet macaws in the 13th–15th centuries and supplied Pueblo communities.
- Turquoise is deliberately omitted: [Thibodeau et al., Science Advances (2018): Was Aztec and Mixtec turquoise mined in the American Southwest?](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aas9370) finds Mesoamerican turquoise consistent with Mesoamerican sources, so a Southwest → Mesoamerica turquoise line is not drawn.

## The Andes and the Amazon

- [UNESCO: Chavín](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/330/), [UNESCO: Tiwanaku](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/567/) and [UNESCO: Qhapaq Ñan, Andean Road System](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1459/). Context for the highland centres and the Inca roads. Spondylus shell, gathered in warm Ecuadorian waters, is found at Chavín and later at Lambayeque, Chimú and Inca sites; the coastal corridor is well supported, the highland links are drawn fainter.
- Caravans between ecological zones: the two-way lines around Tiwanaku, Moquegua, Cochabamba and San Pedro de Atacama represent llama-caravan exchange between highlands, coast and eastern valleys documented by textiles, snuff trays and colonies. They are representative rather than mapped roads.
- Amazonian networks: [Heckenberger et al., Science (2003): Amazonia 1492: pristine forest or cultural parkland?](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1086112) documents large, connected late pre-Columbian settlements in the upper Xingu, and [Britannica: Marajoara culture](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Marajoara-culture) summarizes the mound-building society at the Amazon mouth (about 400–1300 CE) and its elaborate pottery. Santarém (Tapajós) and Marajoara ceramics, riverine exchange along the Amazon, Rio Negro, Casiquiare and Orinoco, and the Arawak-associated spread of ceramics and manioc are drawn as two-way river links marked uncertain: the river network is well attested, individual trade routes are not. Muiraquitã greenstone amulets from the lower Amazon are reported at sites in the Guianas and the Caribbean; that line is a hypothesis. No evidence is known to us for Marajoara pottery reaching the Inca, so no such line is drawn.
- Amazon–Andes links: Chavín imagery of jaguars, caimans and tropical plants, later coca and feather use, and Inca frontier exchange indicate connections with the eastern lowlands, but no cargo route is recovered; these lines are uncertain.
- Metallurgy by sea: [Hosler (1988): Ancient West Mexican metallurgy: South and Central American origins and West Mexican transformations](https://doi.org/10.1525/aa.1988.90.4.02a00030) argues that West Mexican metalworking derives from South and Central American traditions transmitted by maritime contact. This remains a hypothesis and is drawn fainter.

## The Caribbean

- [Nägele et al., Science (2020): Genomic insights into the early peopling of the Caribbean](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba8697) and [Fernandes et al., Nature (2021): A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-03053-2). Ceramic-using people related to Arawak speakers of northeastern South America spread through the Lesser Antilles into the Greater Antilles from around 2,500 years ago; later Taíno populations exchanged widely among the islands. Guanín, a gold-copper alloy prized by the Taíno, came from the mainland, but its supply routes are uncertain.

## Deliberate limits

No claim is made about the volume, frequency or political control of any exchange, nor about direct contact between Mesoamerica and the Andes, which remains unproven. Mesoamerica–Caribbean links, Amazonian river networks, Andean maritime balsa trade and many regional systems are omitted. Modern coastlines are retained; the hexagonal map’s cuts interrupt lines without implying interrupted exchange.

## Settler frontiers (1600 and 1800 panes)

Research checked September 23, 2026. Colonial roads and trails, drawn as schematic corridors between founded towns, missions, forts and mines.

- [UNESCO: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1351/): the silver road from Mexico City through Zacatecas, extended to Santa Fe by Juan de Oñate in 1598.
- Lockhart & Schwartz 1983, *Early Latin America*: the Potosí–Tucumán–Córdoba mule road and the towns of the Paraná (Santa Fe 1573, Buenos Aires refounded 1580).
- Monteiro 1994, *Negros da terra*: the São Paulo bandeiras and the raids on the Guairá reductions in the 1620s–30s.
- Hann 1988, *Apalachee: The Land between the Rivers*: the Florida mission chain from St Augustine to Apalachee (1633).
- Trudel 1973, *The Beginnings of New France*: Tadoussac, Quebec (1608), Trois-Rivières (1634) and Montreal (1642).
- Faragher 1992, *Daniel Boone*: the Wilderness Road (1775) and Ohio River settlement; the Great Wagon Road from Philadelphia.
- [NPS: Natchez Trace Parkway](https://www.nps.gov/natr/) and [NPS: Santa Fe National Historic Trail](https://www.nps.gov/safe/): the Trace as the boatmen's road home (1790s–1810s) and William Becknell's 1821 trail.
- Moulton (ed.) 1983–2001, *The Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition*: the 1804–06 route up the Missouri, over Lemhi Pass and down the Columbia.
- Unruh 1979, *The Plains Across*: overland emigration on the Oregon Trail, 1840–60.
- Hackel 2005, *Children of Coyote, Missionaries of Saint Francis*: the Alta California missions from San Diego (1769) to San Francisco (1776) and beyond; the Portolá expedition set out from Loreto.
- [NPS: El Camino Real de los Tejas](https://www.nps.gov/elte/): Saltillo, Monclova, San Antonio (1718) and Nacogdoches.
- Boxer 1962, *The Golden Age of Brazil*: the Caminho Velho from São Paulo and the Caminho Novo from Rio to the Minas Gerais mines; Holanda 1945, *Monções*: the river monsoons from Porto Feliz to Cuiabá.
- Rock 1985, *Argentina 1516–1987*: the southward fort line of the 1820s (Tandil 1823, Bahía Blanca 1828).

Limitations: these are corridors of settlement, not surveys of particular trails; dates give the span of use. The Santa Fe and Oregon trails and the Pampas forts belong to the decades after 1800 and are shown on the last age of the timeline because the frontier they extended is the same one.

## Forced removals (1800 pane)

Research checked September 23, 2026. Corridors of the removals that followed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and the Long Walk, drawn between the homelands and the destinations, not the many detachments' exact roads.

- [NPS: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail](https://www.nps.gov/trte/): the Cherokee northern land route of 1838–39 from the Georgia and Tennessee stockades through Nashville, Hopkinsville and southern Missouri to Tahlequah; Perdue & Green 2007, *The Cherokee Nation and the Trail of Tears*, on the death toll, in the thousands.
- Foreman 1932, *Indian Removal*: the Choctaw (1831–33), Muscogee (1836–37) and Chickasaw (1837–38) removals through Vicksburg, Memphis and Little Rock to the Choctaw Nation and Fort Gibson.
- Missall & Missall 2004, *The Seminole Wars*: Seminole captives shipped from Tampa Bay to New Orleans and up the Mississippi and Arkansas to Fort Gibson, 1836–42.
- [Potawatomi Trail of Death Association](https://potawatomi-tda.org/): the 1838 march from Twin Lakes, Indiana, through Illinois to eastern Kansas.
- Weslager 1972, *The Delaware Indians*: the Lenape moved from the White River in Indiana to the James Fork of the White River in Missouri (1820–21) and on to the Kansas reserve (1829–31).
- Denetdale 2008, *The Long Walk*: the 1864 marches from Fort Defiance and Canyon de Chelly through Fort Wingate and Albuquerque to Bosque Redondo.

Limitations: each nation moved in many detachments over land and water; the corridors show the main lines only, and the many smaller removals (Ho-Chunk, Sauk and Meskwaki, Wyandot, Shawnee, Miami, Ottawa and others) are not drawn.
